articles.title: Getting Paid to Provide Care: Programs for Family Caregivers
articles.summary: Several programs pay family caregivers - Medicaid self-directed care, Structured Family Caregiving, and some long-term care insurance. Most ask for a log of the care you provide.
articles.content:
# Getting Paid to Provide Care

You may be able to be paid for care you already provide. Programs vary by state, so the fastest way to find and apply for what you qualify for:

## Start here (free help applying)
Call the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116 or visit https://eldercare.acl.gov - it connects you to your local Area Agency on Aging, which will tell you your state's programs and help you apply.

## The main pathways:

## Medicaid Self-Directed / Consumer-Directed Care
Available in nearly every state - the person receiving care can hire and direct their own caregiver, often a family member (typically ~$13-25/hour). Reviewers look for a care plan and a log of hours and tasks for approval and annual renewals - your Care Log in this app is built for that.
Find your state program: https://www.medicaid.gov/medicaid/long-term-services-supports/self-directed-services

## Structured Family Caregiving (SFC)
About 11 states pay a tax-free daily stipend to a live-in family caregiver.
Overview: https://www.medicaidplanningassistance.org/structured-family-caregiving/

## Long-Term Care Insurance
Some policies pay informal (family) caregivers - check for an assessment/care-plan requirement and an elimination period.

## Important
These programs vary by state and change over time. Use the links above for current details where you live, and keep your Care Log up to date as supporting evidence.

articles.title: Preventing Caregiver Burnout: Essential Self-Care Strategies
articles.summary: Learn to recognize the signs of burnout and practical strategies to maintain your own health while caregiving.
articles.content:
# Preventing Caregiver Burnout

Caregiver burnout is a state of physical, emotional, and mental exhaustion. It can happen when you don't get the help you need or try to do more than you're able.

## Warning Signs of Burnout

- Feeling overwhelmed or constantly worried
- Feeling tired often
- Getting too much or too little sleep
- Gaining or losing weight
- Becoming easily irritated or angry
- Losing interest in activities you used to enjoy
- Feeling sad
- Having frequent headaches, bodily pain, or other physical problems
- Abusing alcohol or drugs, including prescription medications

## Prevention Strategies

### 1. Accept Help
When friends or family offer assistance, say yes. Let them help with specific tasks like grocery shopping, lawn care, or sitting with your loved one while you take a break.

### 2. Set Realistic Goals
Break large tasks into smaller steps. Prioritize and tackle what's most important. Recognize that you can't do everything.

### 3. Stay Connected
Make time for friends and family. Social connections provide emotional support and can help prevent isolation.

### 4. Set Personal Health Goals
- Aim for 7-8 hours of sleep
- Exercise regularly (even 10-minute walks help)
- Eat nutritious meals
- Attend your own medical appointments

### 5. Join a Support Group
Talking with others who understand what you're going through can be incredibly validating and helpful.

### 6. Use Respite Care
Respite care provides temporary relief by having someone else care for your loved one. This isn't selfish—it's necessary for sustainable caregiving.

## When to Seek Professional Help

If you experience persistent feelings of sadness, hopelessness, or thoughts of harming yourself or your loved one, seek professional help immediately. Call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988.

## Resources

- Family Caregiver Alliance: (800) 445-8106
- Caregiver Support Line: 1-855-260-3274
- Well Spouse Association: (800) 838-0879

articles.title: Understanding Medicare vs. Medicaid: A Complete Guide
articles.summary: Clear explanation of the differences between Medicare and Medicaid, eligibility requirements, and what each covers.
articles.content:
# Medicare vs. Medicaid: What's the Difference?

Many people confuse Medicare and Medicaid. While both programs help with healthcare costs, they serve different populations and cover different services.

## Medicare

### What It Is
Medicare is federal health insurance for:
- People 65 and older
- People under 65 with certain disabilities
- People with End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)

### What It Covers

**Part A (Hospital Insurance):**
- Inpatient hospital stays
- Skilled nursing facility care
- Hospice care
- Some home health care

**Part B (Medical Insurance):**
- Doctor visits
- Outpatient care
- Medical equipment
- Preventive services

**Part C (Medicare Advantage):**
- Alternative to Original Medicare
- Offered by private companies
- Usually includes Part D

**Part D (Prescription Drug Coverage):**
- Prescription medications
- Offered by private companies

### Costs
- Most people don't pay a premium for Part A
- Part B premium in 2024: $174.70/month (standard)
- Deductibles and coinsurance apply

## Medicaid

### What It Is
Medicaid is a joint federal-state program providing health coverage for:
- Low-income individuals and families
- Pregnant women
- Children
- Elderly adults
- People with disabilities

### What It Covers
Coverage varies by state but typically includes:
- Doctor visits
- Hospital stays
- Long-term care (nursing homes, home care)
- Prescription drugs
- Medical equipment
- Therapies

**Important:** Medicaid covers long-term nursing home care; Medicare does NOT.

### Eligibility
Based on:
- Income (varies by state)
- Assets (for elderly/disabled)
- Citizenship/residency
- Category (pregnant, disabled, elderly, etc.)

### Costs
- Usually no or very low premiums
- Minimal copays
- No deductibles

## Dual Eligible

Some people qualify for BOTH Medicare and Medicaid ("dual eligible"):
- Medicare is primary insurance
- Medicaid covers costs Medicare doesn't
- Medicaid may pay Medicare premiums

## Medicare Savings Programs

If you have Medicare but can't afford premiums/copays, Medicare Savings Programs may help:

1. **Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB)** - Pays Part A & B premiums, deductibles, coinsurance
2. **Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary (SLMB)** - Pays Part B premiums
3. **Qualifying Individual (QI)** - Pays Part B premiums (limited funding)

## How to Apply

**Medicare:**
- Automatic enrollment at 65 if receiving Social Security
- Or apply at ssa.gov or (800) 772-1213

**Medicaid:**
- Apply through your state Medicaid office
- Find your state office: medicaid.gov

## Key Takeaways

| Feature | Medicare | Medicaid |
|---------|----------|----------|
| **Who Runs It** | Federal | State & Federal |
| **Eligibility** | Age 65+ or disabled | Low income |
| **Long-Term Care** | NO | YES |
| **Premiums** | Yes (except Part A) | Minimal/none |
| **Asset Limits** | No | Yes (for elderly) |

## Need Help?

- SHIP (State Health Insurance Assistance Program): Free Medicare counseling (877-839-2675)
- BenefitsCheckUp.org: Screen for programs you may qualify for
- Area Agency on Aging: Find local help (eldercare.acl.gov)

articles.title: Home Safety Modifications: Complete Checklist
articles.summary: Practical guide to making your home safer for someone with mobility issues, dementia, or other health conditions.
articles.content:
# Home Safety Modifications Checklist

Making your home safer can prevent falls, injuries, and allow your loved one to age in place longer.

## General Safety (All Rooms)

### Lighting
- [ ] Install bright bulbs (100-watt equivalent LED)
- [ ] Add nightlights in hallways, bathrooms, bedrooms
- [ ] Place light switches at room entrances
- [ ] Use motion-sensor lights for nighttime safety
- [ ] Eliminate glare from shiny floors

### Floors
- [ ] Remove throw rugs or secure with non-slip backing
- [ ] Repair loose floorboards or carpet
- [ ] Keep walkways clear of clutter, cords, pets
- [ ] Use non-slip floor wax
- [ ] Mark edges of steps with contrasting tape

### Furniture
- [ ] Ensure furniture is sturdy (not tippy)
- [ ] Remove low furniture that's hard to see
- [ ] Arrange furniture to create clear pathways
- [ ] Add armrests to chairs for easier standing

## Bathroom (High Risk for Falls)

### Tub/Shower
- [ ] Install grab bars (not towel bars!) near toilet and in shower
- [ ] Use non-slip mats in tub/shower
- [ ] Add shower chair or transfer bench
- [ ] Install handheld showerhead
- [ ] Remove glass shower doors (use curtain instead)
- [ ] Set water heater to 120°F to prevent burns

### Toilet
- [ ] Install raised toilet seat
- [ ] Add grab bars beside toilet
- [ ] Ensure toilet paper is within easy reach

### General
- [ ] Use nightlight or motion-sensor light
- [ ] Keep medications in labeled, easy-open containers
- [ ] Remove lock from bathroom door (for emergencies)

## Kitchen

### Safety
- [ ] Install automatic shut-off for stove (if wandering/memory issues)
- [ ] Use electric kettle with auto shut-off
- [ ] Store heavy items at waist level
- [ ] Label cabinets with pictures (for dementia)
- [ ] Keep fire extinguisher accessible
- [ ] Install stove knob covers (for dementia)

### Accessibility
- [ ] Add lazy susans in corner cabinets
- [ ] Use reachers for high shelves
- [ ] Ensure good lighting over work areas
- [ ] Provide sturdy step stool with handrail

## Bedroom

- [ ] Adjust bed height (feet flat on floor when sitting)
- [ ] Add bed rails (for support, not restraint)
- [ ] Keep phone/medical alert near bed
- [ ] Use nightlight or motion-sensor light
- [ ] Remove clutter from floor
- [ ] Place commonly used items within reach

## Stairs

- [ ] Install handrails on both sides
- [ ] Ensure handrails extend beyond top and bottom steps
- [ ] Add non-slip treads or strips
- [ ] Improve lighting (top, bottom, switches at both ends)
- [ ] Mark edge of top and bottom steps with contrasting tape
- [ ] Consider stair lift if needed

## For Dementia/Memory Loss

### Wandering Prevention
- [ ] Install alarms on exterior doors
- [ ] Add locks that require keys on both sides (check local fire codes)
- [ ] Place STOP sign on doors you don't want opened
- [ ] Remove car keys if driving is unsafe
- [ ] Enroll in Project Lifesaver or similar program
- [ ] Ensure ID bracelet/necklace is worn

### Reduce Confusion
- [ ] Use labels with words AND pictures
- [ ] Remove or cover mirrors if they cause confusion
- [ ] Simplify environment (reduce clutter)
- [ ] Use contrasting colors (plate vs. table, toilet vs. floor)
- [ ] Display large clock and calendar

### Hazard Reduction
- [ ] Lock up medications, cleaning supplies, tools
- [ ] Remove or lock alcohol
- [ ] Hide car keys
- [ ] Remove or disable stove knobs
- [ ] Cover electrical outlets
- [ ] Install carbon monoxide and smoke detectors

## Emergency Preparedness

- [ ] Post emergency numbers by each phone
- [ ] Keep medical information/medication list accessible
- [ ] Install medical alert system
- [ ] Inform neighbors of situation
- [ ] Keep flashlights/batteries accessible
- [ ] Have backup power for medical equipment

## Financial Assistance for Modifications

- **Medicaid Waiver Programs** - May cover home modifications
- **Veterans Aid & Attendance** - VA benefit for home modifications
- **Area Agency on Aging** - May have loan programs
- **Rebuilding Together** - Free repairs for low-income seniors (rebuildingtogether.org)
- **Home Equity Loan/Line of Credit** - Tax-deductible if medically necessary

## Professional Assessment

Consider hiring an Occupational Therapist to assess your home. They can:
- Identify specific hazards
- Recommend modifications
- Teach safer ways to perform tasks
- May be covered by Medicare with doctor's order

## Quick Wins (Start Here)

1. Remove throw rugs
2. Add nightlights
3. Install grab bars in bathroom
4. Improve lighting
5. Clear clutter from walkways

Remember: Most falls happen at home. These modifications can be life-saving.

articles.title: Navigating Difficult Family Conversations About Caregiving
articles.summary: How to talk with siblings, parents, and family members about caregiving responsibilities, finances, and difficult decisions.
articles.content:
# Navigating Difficult Family Conversations

Family dynamics can become strained when caregiving is involved. Here's how to have productive conversations about challenging topics.

## Common Difficult Conversations

1. **Dividing caregiving responsibilities**
2. **When parent refuses help**
3. **Money and financial decisions**
4. **Moving to assisted living**
5. **End-of-life care**
6. **Unequal sibling participation**

## Before the Conversation

### Prepare Yourself
- Clarify your own thoughts and feelings
- Know what you want from the conversation
- Gather relevant information (medical, financial)
- Choose timing when everyone is calm
- Set realistic expectations

### Set the Stage
- Choose neutral, private location
- Avoid holidays or stressful times
- Allow enough time (don't rush)
- Turn off distractions (TV, phones)
- Include all key decision-makers

## Communication Strategies

### Use "I" Statements
❌ "You never help with Dad."
✅ "I feel overwhelmed caring for Dad alone. I need help."

### Focus on the Problem, Not the Person
❌ "You're selfish and don't care about Mom."
✅ "Mom needs more help than I can provide alone. How can we work together?"

### Listen Actively
- Let others speak without interrupting
- Repeat back what you heard: "So you're saying..."
- Acknowledge their perspective: "I can see why you'd feel that way."
- Ask clarifying questions

### Stay Calm
- Take breaks if emotions run high
- Use "I need a moment" instead of storming out
- Breathe deeply
- Remember: You're on the same team

## Specific Situations

### When Siblings Don't Help

**The Problem:** You're doing most/all the caregiving while siblings do little.

**How to Approach:**
1. Be specific about what you need: "I need someone to take Dad to appointments on Tuesdays" (not "I need more help")
2. Offer options: "Can you handle medical appointments, or would bill-paying work better?"
3. Make it concrete: "Can you commit to one visit per week?"
4. Document expectations in writing
5. Accept that help may look different (time vs. money vs. research)

**If They Still Won't Help:**
- Let go of resentment (it hurts you, not them)
- Consider paid help
- Seek support from others
- Set boundaries: "I can't do X anymore"

### When Parent Refuses Help

**Why They Resist:**
- Fear of losing independence
- Denial about decline
- Don't want to be a burden
- Mistrust of strangers
- Financial concerns

**How to Approach:**
1. Pick your battles (safety issues vs. preferences)
2. Frame as helping YOU: "It would give me peace of mind..."
3. Start small (one helper, one task)
4. Let them stay in control where possible
5. Get creative: "companion" not "caregiver"
6. Sometimes they'll accept help from others more easily

**What to Say:**
- "I'm worried about you" (not "You can't do this anymore")
- "Let's try it for a month" (not "This is how it's going to be")
- "What would help you most?" (ask their input)

### Talking About Money

**Prepare These Questions:**
- What are monthly expenses?
- What income sources exist?
- What assets are available?
- Are there long-term care insurance or VA benefits?
- What are end-of-life wishes?

**Key Documents to Locate:**
- Will
- Power of Attorney (financial, medical)
- Advance Directive/Living Will
- Insurance policies
- Bank accounts
- Property deeds

**Opening the Conversation:**
"I want to make sure we can honor your wishes and provide good care. Can we talk about your finances and plans?"

### Discussing Facility Placement

**When to Consider:**
- Safety concerns (falls, wandering)
- 24/7 supervision needed
- Medical needs beyond family capability
- Caregiver burnout
- Social isolation

**How to Discuss:**
1. Start early (before crisis)
2. Visit places together
3. Emphasize what they'll GAIN (activities, socialization, safety)
4. Acknowledge what they'll lose (independence, familiar surroundings)
5. Make it gradual (adult day care → assisted living → memory care)
6. Respect their timeline when possible

**Phrase It As:**
- "Let's look at options" (not "You have to move")
- "What matters most to you in a living situation?"
- "How can we make this work for everyone?"

## When Conversation Breaks Down

### Family Meeting Not Working?
- Hire a geriatric care manager to facilitate
- Ask social worker or family counselor to mediate
- Use email for "conversations" (gives people time to process)
- Split into smaller groups first
- Take a break and revisit later

### Legal Options When Necessary
- **Guardianship:** Court appoints decision-maker (last resort)
- **Power of Attorney:** Person designates decision-maker (preferred)
- **Mediation:** Neutral third party helps resolve disputes

## Self-Care During Conflict

- Join a caregiver support group
- See a therapist
- Set boundaries: "I can't continue if..."
- Take breaks from caregiving AND family drama
- Remember: You can only control yourself

## Scripts for Common Situations

**Starting a family meeting:**
"Thanks for coming. I wanted us to talk about Mom's care. I've been handling X, Y, Z, and I need help. I'd like us to create a plan together."

**Asking for specific help:**
"I need someone to take Dad to his Tuesday appointments. Sarah, could you handle that, or would Saturday visits work better for you?"

**Setting boundaries:**
"I love Mom, but I can't continue doing everything alone. I need each of you to commit to one specific task."

**Addressing non-participating sibling:**
"I know you live far away and can't help with daily care. Could you handle phone calls to insurance companies and bill-paying instead?"

**When parent resists help:**
"Mom, I'm worried about you being alone all day. Would you be willing to try having someone come twice a week, just to help with cleaning? It would really help me worry less."

## Remember

- **Perfect agreement is rare** - aim for "good enough"
- **You can't change others** - only yourself
- **It's okay to be angry** - but don't make it your fuel
- **Some relationships won't survive** - protect your wellbeing
- **You're doing your best** - that's enough

## Resources

- Family Caregiver Alliance: (800) 445-8106
- Aging Life Care Association (care managers): (520) 881-8008
- Family Mediators: mediate.com

articles.title: End-of-Life Planning: Important Conversations and Documents
articles.summary: A compassionate guide to discussing and planning for end-of-life care, including legal documents and healthcare wishes.
articles.content:
# End-of-Life Planning

While difficult, these conversations and documents can ensure your loved one's wishes are honored and reduce family conflict during already stressful times.

## Essential Legal Documents

### 1. Advance Directive (Living Will)
**What It Is:** Document stating what medical treatments you want/don't want if unable to communicate

**Should Include:**
- CPR wishes
- Ventilator/breathing machine preferences
- Feeding tube decisions
- Dialysis preferences
- Organ donation wishes
- Other specific treatments

**How to Create:**
- Use your state's form (free at caringinfo.org)
- Discuss with doctor
- Give copies to family, doctor, hospital
- Update if wishes change

### 2. Medical Power of Attorney (Healthcare Proxy)
**What It Is:** Names someone to make medical decisions if you can't

**Choosing Your Agent:**
- Someone who knows your wishes
- Can make hard decisions under pressure
- Will advocate for you
- Lives nearby (ideally)

**What They Decide:**
- Treatment options
- Doctors and facilities
- Access to medical records
- End-of-life care

### 3. Financial Power of Attorney
**What It Is:** Names someone to handle financial matters if you can't

**Powers May Include:**
- Paying bills
- Managing investments
- Filing taxes
- Handling benefits
- Selling property

**Types:**
- **Durable:** Takes effect immediately, continues if incapacitated
- **Springing:** Only takes effect if incapacitated

### 4. Will
**What It Is:** Legal document stating how to distribute assets after death

**Should Include:**
- Beneficiaries
- Executor (person handling estate)
- Guardian for minor children
- Specific bequests
- Funeral wishes

### 5. POLST/MOLST Form
**What It Is:** Portable medical orders for seriously ill patients

**Key Features:**
- Bright pink form (easy to find in emergency)
- Signed by doctor
- Details level of care wanted
- Travels with patient
- More detailed than advance directive

**Who Needs It:**
- Seriously ill patients
- Frail elderly
- Anyone who might not want full treatment

## Having the Conversation

### When to Talk
- Before a crisis
- When healthy (if possible)
- After a friend's death
- After news story triggers discussion
- During estate planning

### How to Start
- "I was reading about advance directives. Have you thought about what you'd want?"
- "What matters most to you if you become seriously ill?"
- "Let's make sure I know your wishes so I can honor them."

### Questions to Ask
1. "What does a 'good death' look like to you?"
2. "What's more important: length of life or quality?"
3. "How do you feel about life support?"
4. "Where would you want to be cared for?"
5. "What would make life not worth living?"
6. "What are your fears about dying?"
7. "What would you want us to know?"

### If They Resist
- Don't push too hard
- Come back to it later
- Start with easier topics (funeral wishes)
- Share your own wishes first
- Use hypotheticals: "If you were in a coma with no chance of recovery..."

## Understanding Hospice

### What Is Hospice?
Care focused on comfort (not cure) for people with terminal illness (6 months or less to live)

### What Hospice Provides
- Skilled nursing care
- Medical equipment
- Medications for comfort
- Emotional/spiritual support
- Respite care for family
- Bereavement support (after death)

### Where Hospice Happens
- At home (most common)
- Nursing home
- Hospital
- Inpatient hospice facility

### Cost
- Medicare covers 100% of hospice
- Most private insurance covers it
- Medicaid covers it
- No one is denied due to inability to pay

### Common Myths

**Myth:** "Choosing hospice means giving up."
**Truth:** It means shifting from cure to comfort—often improves quality of remaining life.

**Myth:** "You can't change your mind."
**Truth:** You can leave hospice and return to treatment anytime.

**Myth:** "Hospice shortens life."
**Truth:** Studies show hospice may actually extend life by preventing complications and providing excellent symptom management.

**Myth:** "Hospice is only for the last few days."
**Truth:** Earlier referral (when still relatively well) allows more time to benefit from services.

### When to Consider Hospice
- Frequent hospitalizations
- Declining despite treatment
- More bad days than good
- Spending most time in bed
- Weight loss/weakness
- Doctor mentions "time is limited"

### How to Start
1. Ask doctor for hospice evaluation
2. Hospice agency does assessment (no obligation)
3. If eligible, can start same day
4. Revocable any time

## Practical Planning

### Funeral/Memorial Planning
**Pre-Planning Benefits:**
- Ensures wishes are followed
- Removes burden from family
- Can pre-pay (locks in costs)
- Prevents family disagreement

**Decisions to Make:**
- Burial vs. cremation
- Type of service
- Location of service
- Readings, music, speakers
- Obituary wishes
- Organ donation

**Cost-Saving Tips:**
- Compare prices (required by law)
- Simple casket ($700 vs. $5000+)
- Direct cremation ($1000-$3000)
- Memorial service later (not funeral)
- Skip embalming if not required
- Use cremation container instead of casket
- Donate body to science (free)

### Important Information to Document
Create a "When I Die" file with:

**Legal/Financial:**
- Location of will, POA, advance directive
- Bank accounts, credit cards
- Insurance policies
- Property deeds
- Passwords (bank, email, social media)
- Safe deposit box location/key

**Benefits/Accounts:**
- Social Security number
- Medicare/Medicaid numbers
- Veterans benefits
- Pensions
- Investment accounts

**Contacts:**
- Lawyer
- Financial advisor
- Insurance agent
- Executor
- Doctors

**Final Wishes:**
- Funeral preferences
- Burial location
- Organ donation
- Who to notify
- Charitable donations
- Special requests

### Digital Legacy
- Grant access to email, social media
- Specify what to do with accounts (memorialize, delete)
- List online accounts and passwords
- Share locations of photos, documents

## Supporting Someone at End of Life

### What to Say
- "I love you"
- "Thank you for..."
- "I forgive you" / "I'm sorry"
- "You can let go"
- Read favorite prayers, poems, passages
- Share memories
- Give permission to die

### What NOT to Say
- "Don't give up"
- "You have to fight this"
- "Everything will be fine"
- "At least..."

### Physical Comfort
- Keep lips moist
- Turn gently every 2 hours
- Play favorite music
- Reduce noise
- Soft lighting
- Cool compresses for fever
- Light blankets

### Signs Death is Near (Days to Hours)
- Sleeping more, hard to wake
- Less interested in food/drink
- Confusion about time/place/people
- Cool hands and feet
- Irregular breathing (pauses)
- Restlessness
- Talking to deceased loved ones

### At the Moment of Death
- No need to call 911 (if on hospice or expected)
- Call hospice nurse (if on hospice)
- Take time with body (no rush)
- Call funeral home when ready
- Notify family

## After Death

### First 24 Hours
- Call funeral home
- Notify immediate family
- If veteran: call (800) 827-1000 for burial benefits
- Secure home and valuables
- Care for pets

### First Week
- Plan funeral/memorial
- Order death certificates (need 10-15)
- Contact Social Security (stops benefits)
- Contact banks, credit cards
- Notify employer, insurance

### First Month
- File will with probate court
- Contact attorney if needed
- Notify creditors
- Cancel subscriptions, memberships
- Forward mail
- Return medical equipment

## Resources

- National Hospice and Palliative Care: (800) 658-8898
- Aging with Dignity (Five Wishes advance directive): (888) 594-7437
- Caring Info (state-specific forms): caringinfo.org
- National Funeral Directors: nfda.org
- Social Security Death Benefits: (800) 772-1213

## Self-Care for Caregivers

End-of-life caregiving is emotionally exhausting. Remember:
- Anticipatory grief is normal
- Take breaks (respite care)
- Accept help
- Join support group
- See therapist if needed
- Let go of guilt
- Find meaning in this time together

## Final Thoughts

These conversations are gifts—to your loved one (honoring their wishes) and to yourself (clarity and peace of mind). While difficult, they're acts of love.

Start small. Ask one question. Fill out one form. Every step helps.
